lesson.title: A Promise for Every Flow: Integrated Services and Why It Didn't Scale
lesson.summary: Integrated Services (IntServ) grants explicit, per-flow resource reservations negotiated end to end through RSVP signaling, offering far more precise guarantees than DiffServ at the cost of every router remembering every flow it carries.
lesson.body:
A brief note on ordering is worth making honestly before anything else: this unit covers DiffServ before IntServ, but historically IntServ came first, defined in the early to mid 1990s as the internet's first serious QoS architecture proposal. DiffServ, covered in the previous chapter, was developed afterward specifically as a scalable alternative once IntServ's fundamental scaling limitation, unpacked below, became apparent. IntServ is covered second here because its fine-grained, stateful approach is easier to appreciate by direct contrast with the coarse, stateless approach DiffServ takes, which the previous chapter already laid out.

The mechanism itself is fine-grained by design. An application wanting a real guarantee describes its expected traffic using a flow specification, shaped in practice exactly like the r and b parameters of a token bucket covered earlier in this unit, then signals that specification hop by hop along the path to the receiver using RSVP, the Resource Reservation Protocol. At every router along that path, an admission control check, covered two chapters back, tests whether granting this new reservation is actually possible given everything already committed to other flows. If every single hop along the entire path says yes, the flow is admitted, and each of those routers now holds state describing exactly how much of its own scheduling and buffer resources are set aside for that specific flow, enforcing it going forward using the same scheduling disciplines covered earlier, for instance a dedicated queue or a guaranteed transmission slot reserved just for that reservation.

IntServ actually defines two real service classes worth naming. Guaranteed Service provides a mathematically bounded worst-case delay, intended for applications with genuinely hard real-time requirements. Controlled-Load Service is looser and cheaper to provide: it aims to give a flow performance close to what it would experience on a lightly loaded, uncongested network, without offering a hard mathematical bound on delay.

The scaling failure is concrete, not abstract, and it comes down to state. A DiffServ core router needs one small table keyed by DSCP value, at most a handful of entries. An IntServ core router carrying, say, a million concurrent flows needs a million individual reservation records sitting in memory, must process periodic RSVP refresh messages for every single one of them, and must run an admission control computation on every new flow setup request that arrives. That is a fundamentally different order of computational and memory burden than DiffServ's approach, and critically, it grows directly with the number of flows crossing a link, not with the number of service classes offered. This is exactly why IntServ has mostly stayed confined to edge networks, private wide area links, and specific enterprise deployments where flow counts are modest and manageable, rather than the internet's core, which is precisely where DiffServ's stateless marking was designed to operate instead.
